Bolt torque: general purpose values for plain steel fasteners
Dry, unplated or zinc plated, into a steel joint, at roughly 75 percent of proof load. Lubricated threads (oil, anti-seize, moly) reduce the required torque by about 25 percent for the same clamp load; use the lubricated column or the manufacturer's K factor. Flange bolting, gasket joints, and any joint with a specified torque use that specification, not this table. Fastener depth, thread engagement, and joint design are in ButtonUp.

The torque formula, and why lubrication matters
T = K × D × F
T = torque, D = nominal bolt diameter, F = target clamp load
K ≈ 0.20 dry plain steel   0.15 zinc plated or lightly oiled   0.12 moly or anti-seize

Same torque with K 0.12 instead of 0.20 gives 1.67 times the clamp load: enough to yield the bolt or crush the gasket.
  • Torque is a proxy for clamp load, and 80 to 90 percent of it goes into friction. Thread condition changes clamp load more than any other single thing.
  • Torque in steps: 30, 60, 100 percent, star pattern on flanges and bearing caps, then a final pass at 100 to confirm.
  • Stainless on stainless galls. Anti-seize and the lubricated value, always.
  • Reused bolts that have been torqued to yield (torque-to-yield, some engine and structural applications) are not reused.
Field tip: calibrate the wrench, then calibrate yourselfA click wrench that has lived in a toolbox for five years reads wrong. Check it on a tester yearly. Then check yourself: torque a bolt to the table value with the wrench, then loosen it with a beam wrench and see what it took. The number surprises most people the first time.

Bearing fits: which ring is tight depends on which ring rotates relative to the load
A ring that rotates relative to the load direction needs an interference fit or it creeps and frets. A ring that is stationary relative to the load can be a transition or clearance fit. On a normal motor or pump (rotating shaft, stationary housing, load direction fixed) the inner ring is tight on the shaft and the outer ring is a close slide in the housing. These are general guidance grades; the bearing manufacturer catalogue gives the exact grade for the bearing size, load, and application.

Widely used general industry values. Acceptable is the most misalignment a machine should run with; excellent is the target on a new installation or a critical machine. Rim and face correction math
Offset at the coupling = rim reading ÷ 2 (with sag corrected)
Angularity = face reading ÷ coupling face diameter (gap difference per unit diameter)
Foot correction = offset + angularity × distance from coupling to that foot

Example: rim 0.20 mm TIR, face 0.10 mm over 200 mm diameter, inboard foot 300 mm, outboard foot 800 mm from coupling
Offset = 0.10 mm; angularity = 0.0005 mm/mm
Inboard shim change = 0.10 + 0.0005 × 300 = 0.25 mm
Outboard shim change = 0.10 + 0.0005 × 800 = 0.50 mm
Sign convention and which machine moves are set at the start and written down. A laser system does this arithmetic; the value of knowing it is being able to check the laser when the answer looks wrong.

Shim rules
  • No more than four or five shims under any foot. A tall stack springs. Replace many thin shims with one thick one.
  • Thickest shims against the base, thinnest at the top of the stack, next to the foot.
  • Stainless pre-cut shims, clean and flat. No burrs, no bent tabs, no rust, no paint. A shim with a burr is a soft foot.
  • Shim covers the whole foot, with the slot around the bolt. A shim under half a foot is an angled foot.
  • Measure every shim with a micrometer before it goes in. Nominal thickness is nominal.
  • Write the stack down: foot, thicknesses, total. It goes in the equipment record.
Feeler gauge sets and dial indicator sag
  • Standard inch feeler set: 0.0015 to 0.025 in in 0.001 steps. Metric: 0.05 to 1.00 mm. Combine leaves to make intermediate sizes; the sum is the reading.
  • Feeler gauge for soft foot: 0.002 in (0.05 mm) should not enter under any foot with the bolt loose. If it enters, that foot is soft.
  • Indicator bracket sag: mount the bracket and indicator on a straight bar, zero at the top, rotate to the bottom. The reading is twice the sag. Correct rim readings by adding the sag to the bottom reading. A long bracket on a small shaft can sag 0.05 mm or more, which is the whole tolerance at 1800 rpm.
  • Indicator on a face reading: no sag correction needed, but the indicator must be square to the face and the hub must not float axially between readings. Check axial float and hold the shaft against one end.
Field tip: the shim you cannot find is under the last motorShims go in and come out of a labelled bag or box for that machine. At the end of the job, the count matches. A shim on the floor of the base ends up under the next motor and gives it a soft foot that nobody can explain.

Grease quantity and interval
Quantity G (grams) = 0.005 × D × B   (D = bearing OD mm, B = width mm)
6205: 0.005 × 52 × 15 = 3.9 g   6309: 0.005 × 100 × 25 = 12.5 g   22220: 0.005 × 180 × 46 = 41 g

A standard hand grease gun delivers roughly 1 to 1.5 g per stroke. Weigh yours once: pump ten strokes onto a scale.
  • Interval: the bearing manufacturer's chart by bearing type, bore, and speed, then shortened for temperature (halve it for every 15°C above 70°C), contamination, vertical shafts, and vibration.
  • Rough guide for a horizontal ball bearing at 1800 rpm in a clean, cool location: 40 mm bore, roughly 6 months; 80 mm bore, roughly 3 months. Roller bearings and 3600 rpm: half that. Small sealed bearings: never.
  • Grease compatibility: lithium with lithium complex is fine; lithium or lithium complex with polyurea is not; calcium sulphonate is compatible with most. Check the chart before changing product, and purge if in doubt.

Pipe sizes, schedule 40 wall, and class 150 flange bolting
